what-is-an-operating-system.title: Mechanism and policy are separate decisions
what-is-an-operating-system.body: A mechanism provides a capability: a timer interrupt makes preemption possible, a page table controls memory access, and a run queue records eligible tasks. A policy decides how to use it: which task runs next, how much memory each owner receives, or when writes reach storage. Keeping these ideas separate explains how two systems can use similar hardware yet deliver different fairness, latency, and power behavior.

what-is-an-operating-system.title: The kernel and the rest of the operating system
what-is-an-operating-system.body: The kernel is the privileged resource manager. An operating-system distribution also includes libraries, service managers, command interpreters, utilities, and configuration. A shell interprets a command but normally asks the kernel to create processes and open files. A graphical desktop is another user-space program. A failure in one service does not necessarily mean the kernel failed, although that service may be essential to useful operation.

what-is-an-operating-system.title: Protection boundaries and controlled sharing
what-is-an-operating-system.body: Isolation means one task cannot freely read another task's memory or overwrite the kernel. Controlled sharing is still necessary: files, pipes, sockets, and shared mappings make cooperation possible through defined interfaces. The kernel checks authority when creating or using these relationships. A process boundary is therefore not an absolute prohibition on communication; it makes communication and resource access subject to explicit rules.

what-is-an-operating-system.title: Evaluate a design through guarantees
what-is-an-operating-system.body: For a file-saving operation, ask four separate questions: who may open the file, whether concurrent writes can interleave, when another process can observe the new data, and when the data survives power loss. Access checks, synchronization, visibility, and durability require different mechanisms. An OS abstraction is useful because it offers a contract, but calling an operation successfully only proves the guarantees that its contract actually promises.

what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.title: Resolve the command and create the child
what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.body: For a typical external command, a Unix shell searches its configured command path unless a pathname was provided, prepares redirections, and creates a child execution. Built-in commands can run inside the shell instead. The parent and child must distinguish the return from process creation: the parent receives a child identifier, the child receives zero, and failure leaves no child to execute or wait for.

what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.title: Replace the image without replacing the identity
what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.body: Successful exec replaces the current program's mappings and execution state; it does not create another process identifier. The executable's loadable segments establish code and data mappings, and the initial stack communicates arguments and environment. Descriptors marked close-on-exec are closed while others can survive. This is how a shell connects a child's standard output to a pipe before the new program begins.

what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.title: Dynamic linking and language startup
what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.body: When an executable requests a dynamic interpreter, that loader maps needed shared objects and performs the relocations required by the binary interface. Some symbol resolution may be deferred, depending on configuration. Runtime initialization then establishes language facilities before application entry. A missing shared library can therefore prevent a program from reaching main even though the executable file exists and the kernel accepted its format.

what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.title: Trace completion and distinguish failure stages
what-happens-when-you-run-a-program.body: Consider a command whose executable cannot be found, whose loader fails, and whose main returns status 7. These failures occur at different stages and can produce different shell diagnostics and statuses. A supervising parent waits for its child and interprets normal exit separately from signal termination. In a pipeline, each stage has its own process and status; the shell's reported pipeline status follows its configured policy.

course-environment.title: Build a small inspectable C program
course-environment.body: Start with one source file that prints its PID and exits. Compile with debug information and warnings, for example cc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -g demo.c -o demo, adjusting platform-specific flags deliberately. Fix compiler warnings before adding concurrency. Debug information lets tools relate instructions to source; it does not prevent optimization from rearranging execution, so record optimization flags when comparing behavior.

course-environment.title: Separate correctness runs from performance runs
course-environment.body: Memory and undefined-behavior sanitizers can expose invalid accesses, use-after-free, and selected arithmetic errors. Their instrumentation changes timing and memory use, so use a separate uninstrumented build for performance measurement. Thread sanitizers detect many data races but cannot prove absence of every deadlock or logical race. A passing instrumented run is evidence about exercised paths, not a mathematical proof of the whole program.

course-environment.title: Know what the host permits you to observe
course-environment.body: Profiling, packet capture, kernel tracing, and reading another process's details can require permissions that ordinary compilation does not. A container or managed VM may expose fewer counters or restrict tracing. Treat a permission error as an environment property instead of concluding that the operating-system mechanism is absent. Record the attempted observation, the returned error, and an alternative user-space measurement if one can answer the question.

course-environment.title: Make an experiment reproducible
course-environment.body: Keep the source, executable build command, input, expected result, actual output, and environment description together. For a scheduling experiment, include worker count, CPU affinity if changed, and background load. For file I/O, include file size and whether the cache was warm. Run a known-good baseline first; otherwise a configuration difference can look like a new kernel behavior when the programs were never comparable.

c-survival-guide-for-os.title: Represent sizes and errors with the right types
c-survival-guide-for-os.body: Buffer capacities use size_t, while operations such as read return ssize_t so negative errors remain representable. Check a negative result before converting it to an unsigned size. If read returns -1 and code converts that to size_t, it can become an enormous positive value. Test multiplication before allocating count times element_size, since overflow can allocate a small buffer that later receives a much larger logical write.

c-survival-guide-for-os.title: Ownership across branches and error paths
c-survival-guide-for-os.body: Every successful resource acquisition needs a defined release: malloc pairs with free, an opened descriptor with close, and a joined thread with the appropriate lifecycle handling. Initialize handles to an invalid sentinel and release only acquired resources. A cleanup path should also preserve the original failure information. Releasing an object twice is incorrect even when a second cleanup branch was intended to be defensive.

c-survival-guide-for-os.title: Strings, bytes, and structures are different formats
c-survival-guide-for-os.body: A byte buffer returned by read is not automatically a C string. String functions require a terminating zero within accessible storage, while binary data may contain zeros anywhere. A C structure can contain padding and platform-dependent integer representation, so sending sizeof(struct) bytes is not a portable protocol. Encode lengths and integer byte order explicitly when another process or machine must interpret the data.

c-survival-guide-for-os.title: Undefined behavior defeats source-level predictions
c-survival-guide-for-os.body: Reading an object after its lifetime ends, accessing beyond an array, or introducing an unsynchronized conflicting access can invalidate assumptions about generated code. volatile does not make a counter increment atomic or establish cross-thread synchronization. Use the language's atomic facilities or locks with a documented ownership rule. First establish a valid C program; measuring an undefined program repeatedly does not turn its observed behavior into a guarantee.

essential-system-tools.title: Process identity and sampling
essential-system-tools.body: Use process listings to establish the PID, parent, command, and state, then choose an interval-based view for changes. A PID can be reused after exit, so correlate start time as well as its numeric value during long investigations. One snapshot cannot distinguish a brief burst from sustained saturation. Collect a few comparable intervals and relate them to the exact workload event rather than a recollection of when things felt slow.

essential-system-tools.title: CPU and memory views answer different questions
essential-system-tools.body: CPU percentages describe execution consumption under a tool's normalization rules. A process can exceed 100 percent when the tool counts several CPUs separately. Resident memory measures a different resource and can include shared mappings. A rising virtual size may be reservation rather than resident allocation. Read each tool's units and denominator before comparing percentages or adding memory values across processes.

essential-system-tools.title: Trace the boundary, then profile the computation
essential-system-tools.body: A syscall trace can reveal repeated failed opens, short reads, or long blocking waits. If requests are slow while syscalls complete quickly, sample the application's CPU execution to locate computation. Conversely a CPU profile may look sparse when nearly all elapsed time is spent waiting. Choose on-CPU, off-CPU, or syscall evidence according to the hypothesis; one tool is not a universal explanation of latency.

essential-system-tools.title: Use a hypothesis and a falsifying observation
essential-system-tools.body: Suppose an endpoint is slow because a worker is allegedly CPU-bound. Predict high worker CPU use and significant runnable demand. If CPU use is low and workers wait on sockets, the evidence contradicts that explanation. Next inspect dependency latency and socket behavior. State what would disprove a hypothesis before changing configuration; otherwise every new counter can be interpreted as support for the first guess.

how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.title: Fetch, decode, execute, and retire
how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.body: The program counter identifies the instruction stream. Fetch supplies instruction bytes, decode interprets operations and operands, execution performs work, and retirement makes completed work architecturally visible in the required manner. These stages can overlap in a pipeline. A load might wait for memory while an independent addition executes, but an addition that needs that load's result must wait for the dependency.

how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.title: Registers, flags, and control flow
how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.body: General-purpose registers hold operands and addresses; stack and instruction pointers support execution flow; status information records conditions used by branches. A call and return follow the machine's instruction semantics plus the ABI's register and stack conventions. The OS must preserve the execution state needed across a task switch. Saving only the source-level variables would miss registers, control state, and suspended kernel execution.

how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.title: Pipelines do not remove dependencies
how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.body: In a simplified four-stage pipeline, four independent instructions need seven stage-times from an empty pipeline to final completion, assuming one instruction enters each time and no stalls. This is an illustration of overlap, not a claim about a particular CPU's instruction throughput. A branch misprediction or cache miss can interrupt the ideal pattern. Throughput after filling and latency of one instruction are different measurements.

how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.title: Interruptible execution and precise state
how-the-cpu-executes-instructions.body: When an interrupt or exception transfers control, software needs an architectural state from which it can resume or report failure. Speculative internal work is not automatically committed application progress. The saved instruction position and exception semantics determine whether execution retries an operation or continues elsewhere. This boundary lets the kernel schedule and handle faults without requiring application code to explicitly yield after every machine instruction.

privilege-levels.title: CPU privilege and user identity are independent axes
privilege-levels.body: User mode and kernel mode describe processor authority, while a user identifier describes whose access policy applies. A privileged account's application normally still executes in user mode until it requests a kernel service. Conversely kernel code serving an ordinary user's request must honor that user's permissions. Confusing these axes leads to the false claim that a root process continuously executes arbitrary kernel instructions.

privilege-levels.title: Protected operations require controlled entry
privilege-levels.body: Updating privileged translation registers, configuring interrupts, and directly controlling some devices are restricted by the architecture and OS configuration. A user instruction attempting a prohibited operation typically causes an exception rather than silently acquiring permission. System calls enter approved kernel paths with a defined calling convention. The caller supplies requests and arguments, not an arbitrary privileged instruction sequence for the kernel to trust.

privilege-levels.title: Validate memory and lifetime across the boundary
privilege-levels.body: A user pointer can name an inaccessible page, overflow when combined with a length, or refer to data modified by another thread. Kernel interfaces therefore copy or validate data using mechanisms appropriate to user memory and operation semantics. Checking a pathname once is not sufficient if later code resolves a different mutable pathname. Protection includes avoiding time-of-check/time-of-use inconsistencies, not just testing a permission bit.

privilege-levels.title: Example: opening a restricted file
privilege-levels.body: An application requests an open operation while running in user mode. The CPU transfers control to the syscall entry, and kernel code resolves the path and evaluates credentials and permissions. Access denial returns an error and execution resumes in user mode. The transition to kernel mode happened in both allowed and denied cases; it did not grant the requesting process permission to read the restricted contents.

the-memory-hierarchy.title: Capacity, latency, and bandwidth trade off
the-memory-hierarchy.body: Registers hold immediate working operands; cache levels retain recently used memory lines; DRAM holds a larger active working set; persistent storage supplies still larger backing data. Exact sizes and timings depend on the machine. Latency measures delay for an access, while bandwidth measures volume transferred per interval. A workload with many independent requests can achieve substantial bandwidth even when one dependent request still experiences high latency.

the-memory-hierarchy.title: A simple average-access calculation
the-memory-hierarchy.body: Assume a cache hit costs 2 time units and a miss costs an additional 80 units before the access completes. With a 5 percent miss rate, average access cost is 2 + 0.05 times 80 = 6 units in this simplified model. Increasing the miss rate to 10 percent raises it to 10. The calculation assumes additive penalties and ignores overlap, but shows why a small miss-rate change can matter.

the-memory-hierarchy.title: Cache associativity and conflict misses
the-memory-hierarchy.body: A cache maps memory lines into sets. A set can retain only a limited number of lines, determined by associativity, even when other sets are empty. Repeatedly accessing too many addresses that map to one set can cause conflict misses without exhausting total cache capacity. Changing layout or traversal can reduce those conflicts. A larger total cache is not the only possible remedy.

the-memory-hierarchy.title: Coherence is not the same as synchronization
the-memory-hierarchy.body: Coherent caches coordinate visibility of writes to shared cache lines among processors. They do not make a multi-instruction critical section indivisible or supply every ordering required by a language memory model. Two threads can still lose increments while the hardware remains coherent. Use atomic operations or synchronization for correctness, then consider cache placement and false sharing as performance concerns.

interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.title: Asynchronous versus instruction-caused events
interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.body: An external device interrupt can arrive independently of the instruction currently executing. An exception is associated with execution, such as an invalid instruction or translation failure. The word trap is used differently across architectures and textbooks, including deliberate service entry and a class of post-instruction exception. State the convention before comparing them; all three should not be described as ordinary asynchronous device notifications.

interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.title: Handler entry and bounded immediate work
interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.body: The processor identifies a handler through the architecture's configured entry mechanism and preserves the state required by its contract. The handler determines the event source, records or acknowledges necessary state, and performs urgent work. Longer work may be deferred to a schedulable context. The exact split is platform-dependent, but its purpose is to avoid holding up other urgent events while doing arbitrary lengthy processing.

interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.title: Masking, nesting, and concurrency
interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.body: Masking some interrupts delays their handling under the processor's rules; it does not automatically stop another CPU from accessing shared memory. Some events are not maskable through ordinary mechanisms. A handler and a normal thread can therefore race on shared state even when each looks sequential in isolation. Protect the actual participants and context, including possible re-entry, rather than assuming an interrupt handler has exclusive use of the machine.

interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.title: Example: a timer wakeup is not immediate execution
interrupts-exceptions-and-traps.body: A sleeping task has a deadline. A timer event leads the kernel to mark it runnable when the wait condition is satisfied. If a higher-priority task is executing or the CPU is busy, the awakened task may run later. Measured sleep duration can exceed the requested interval. The timer event, transition to runnable state, and eventual dispatch are three separate points on the latency timeline.

what-the-kernel-manages.title: Execution and address spaces
what-the-kernel-manages.body: The kernel tracks schedulable tasks, chooses where they run, and manages their address-space mappings and access permissions. It resolves faults according to mapping policy and backing storage. A task's virtual address is interpreted using its current translation context, so identical numeric addresses need not reference identical physical memory. Sharing requires an explicit relationship between mappings or other objects, not merely matching addresses.

what-the-kernel-manages.title: Files, devices, and protocol state
what-the-kernel-manages.body: File systems organize persistent objects, while drivers translate generic requests into device-specific operations. Networking maintains sockets, buffers, timers, routing information, and transport state. These subsystems interact: receiving a request can wake a task, allocate memory, and cause file I/O. A kernel resource manager therefore coordinates dependency chains rather than treating scheduling, memory, and devices as unrelated services.

what-the-kernel-manages.title: Lifetime, reference counts, and pending work
what-the-kernel-manages.body: An object may remain alive after one owner closes its reference because another reference or outstanding operation still needs it. Conversely an integer handle can be reused for a different object after close. Correct code tracks object identity and operation completion rather than assuming a stored integer always refers to the original resource. This distinction matters in asynchronous I/O, descriptor passing, and concurrent cancellation.

what-the-kernel-manages.title: Policy enforcement and accounting boundaries
what-the-kernel-manages.body: Credentials determine permitted operations; resource limits constrain consumption; accounting records ownership and usage. A container can have an apparent abundance of host memory while its control group has a smaller enforced budget. Similarly a process can hit its descriptor limit before the system-wide capacity is exhausted. Identify the enforcing boundary and the charged resource before increasing an unrelated limit.

kernel-architectures.title: Monolithic does not mean one indivisible source file
kernel-architectures.body: A monolithic kernel can have clean internal interfaces and dynamically loadable modules while its major services still execute within one privileged address space. A module crash or memory corruption can therefore affect the whole kernel. Modularity concerns how code is organized and loaded; isolation concerns which accesses the system prevents. Good source organization alone does not create a hardware-enforced fault boundary.

kernel-architectures.title: Microkernel paths and user-space servers
kernel-architectures.body: A microkernel retains a smaller set of privileged mechanisms and places selected services in separate processes. A file operation may involve messages to a file-system server and a driver server, along with scheduling and memory-transfer mechanisms. That separation can support restart and reduced authority, but recovery still requires handling clients waiting on the failed server. Isolation is useful only with a complete lifecycle and recovery design.

kernel-architectures.title: Hybrid is a descriptive family, not a formula
kernel-architectures.body: Hybrid systems combine architectural choices for compatibility, performance, and service placement. The label does not specify a fixed number of privileged services or predict the cost of a syscall. To compare designs, draw the actual execution path and mark address-space boundaries, permissions, copies, and messages. Two systems described with the same label may make very different choices for drivers or file-system services.

kernel-architectures.title: Worked trade-off: restart a failing driver
kernel-architectures.body: If a driver runs with full kernel memory access, an invalid write may damage unrelated state before recovery is possible. A separately protected driver can have a narrower failure domain, but clients still need timeouts, operation identifiers, and rules for uncertain completion after restart. A storage write that reached the device before the driver crashed cannot simply be assumed absent. Architecture changes failure containment, not the need for correct operation semantics.

system-calls.title: API, ABI, and syscall number
system-calls.body: A source-level API names functions and their types; an ABI specifies their binary calling conventions; a syscall interface defines how requests enter the kernel. The libc function exposed to a program can adapt arguments or choose a different kernel mechanism. Syscall numbers and register assignments depend on architecture. Hardcoding one machine's convention into portable application code confuses the API with a particular implementation boundary.

system-calls.title: Return values and partial effects
system-calls.body: A successful write can report fewer bytes than requested, and failure does not universally mean no earlier effect occurred. The caller must read the operation's contract, preserve progress, and choose whether retrying is safe. A wrapper often communicates failure through a sentinel and errno, but not every library follows that convention. Examine the returned status before inspecting errno, whose previous value can remain after success.

system-calls.title: Descriptor-based operations and authority
system-calls.body: Opening a pathname resolves a name and produces a reference to a kernel-managed object. Later descriptor operations act on that reference, which may survive a rename or removal of a directory entry. This avoids repeating the same name resolution for every access but requires explicit lifetime management. An inherited or passed descriptor can convey access even when the receiving process could not independently open the original path.

system-calls.title: Cost reduction without changing semantics
system-calls.body: Combining many tiny writes into a larger write can reduce entries and copying overhead, but introduces buffering delay and changes how partial progress is handled. An interface that uses shared submission queues may reduce repeated entry overhead while retaining kernel validation and completion rules. Optimize the measured boundary cost, and preserve ordering, error reporting, and durability requirements rather than assuming fewer syscalls automatically means correct faster software.

inside-a-system-call.title: Prepare the user-side request
inside-a-system-call.body: The caller places arguments according to the platform ABI, and a wrapper uses the instruction sequence appropriate to that architecture. Pointers still reference user memory; they are not trusted merely because a library supplied them. Before entry, application buffering or conversion may already have happened. A trace beginning at kernel entry therefore omits time spent formatting, allocating, or waiting on a user-space lock.

inside-a-system-call.title: Validate, acquire, and operate
inside-a-system-call.body: The kernel identifies the operation, obtains referenced objects, checks arguments and access, and coordinates concurrent state with appropriate synchronization. Validation can fail before any device activity. If work must wait, the kernel arranges a wakeup condition and deschedules the task rather than spinning indefinitely. Resource references must remain valid across that wait even if another task closes a related handle or changes external state.

inside-a-system-call.title: Resume and return with observable results
inside-a-system-call.body: Completion makes the task runnable; dispatch later resumes its kernel continuation. The kernel finishes the operation, copies permitted results to user memory, releases temporary resources, and returns through the architecture's exit path. A pending signal can alter what user code observes according to restart and interruption rules. Resumption of kernel work and return to the next user instruction are distinct events.

inside-a-system-call.title: Worked latency accounting
inside-a-system-call.body: Suppose an operation spends 0.1 ms entering and validating, waits 12 ms for I/O, then waits 2 ms runnable before spending 0.2 ms completing. Elapsed latency is 14.3 ms, but kernel CPU execution in this simplified trace is only 0.3 ms. Reducing entry overhead by half saves little compared with removing the I/O or runnable delay. A timing measurement must identify which intervals it includes.

boot-elf-and-the-abi.title: Boot stages and the first user-space process
boot-elf-and-the-abi.body: On a typical Linux boot, firmware hands off to a loader or compatible kernel entry, the kernel initializes critical hardware and memory management, and an initial user-space environment may prepare the real root file system. The system then starts its init or service manager. Exact paths vary with firmware, image configuration, and boot method. Diagnose a failure at its actual stage rather than treating every startup failure as a shell problem.

boot-elf-and-the-abi.title: ELF sections and segments serve different consumers
boot-elf-and-the-abi.body: ELF sections organize information useful to linking and inspection, such as symbols and relocation data. Program headers describe segments needed for execution, including loadable regions and an optional interpreter. The loader works from execution-oriented metadata rather than copying each section independently. A stripped executable can still run because many debugging and symbolic details are unnecessary for establishing its loadable image.

boot-elf-and-the-abi.title: ABI obligations at a function boundary
boot-elf-and-the-abi.body: An ABI specifies where arguments and return values appear, which registers a callee must preserve, stack alignment, and other binary conventions. If assembly code corrupts a preserved register, its caller can fail far away from the call. Structure layout and integer sizes also matter across binary boundaries. Matching function names is insufficient when separately compiled modules disagree on the calling convention or data representation.

boot-elf-and-the-abi.title: Static, dynamic, and position-independent execution
boot-elf-and-the-abi.body: Static linking places required object code into the executable according to linker choices; dynamic linking resolves dependencies through shared objects at load time or later. Position-independent code supports placement at different addresses without assuming one fixed location. ASLR changes placement policy but does not eliminate relocations or ABI requirements. A correct deployment must provide compatible dependencies as well as an executable with a recognized file format.

program-vs-process.title: Creation introduces an execution identity
program-vs-process.body: A program stored on disk is passive until the system establishes an execution context for it. The resulting process has an identifier, ownership, mappings, open resources, and one or more threads. Loading another instance creates another identity. Replacing an existing process image with exec changes the executed program while retaining the process identity, demonstrating why program and process are not interchangeable terms.

program-vs-process.title: Private mappings can share physical pages
program-vs-process.body: Two processes can map the same executable file's read-only code pages. Their virtual address spaces still have separate mapping and permission contexts. Private writable data may initially share backing pages through copy-on-write and diverge when either process writes. Physical sharing therefore does not necessarily mean application-visible shared variables; the mapping semantics determine whether a write becomes visible to the other process.

program-vs-process.title: Resources are not all private by default
program-vs-process.body: A child can inherit descriptors that refer to the same open file descriptions as its parent. Their file offsets may therefore interact even though ordinary variables are private after fork. Explicit shared memory creates another sharing relationship. To predict communication or interference, list each resource separately: address space, descriptor table, underlying file object, working directory, and credentials can follow different inheritance and sharing rules.

program-vs-process.title: Worked identity exercise
program-vs-process.body: A supervisor with PID 400 creates child 401, and the child successfully execs a worker executable. The worker is still process 401; no third process was created by exec. The supervisor can wait for 401 even though the child runs different code now. If the supervisor independently launches another worker, that execution has another identifier and lifecycle even when both workers map identical instruction bytes.

the-process-control-block.title: Identity, scheduling, and accounting fields
the-process-control-block.body: A conceptual PCB records process identity and relationships, execution state, scheduling priority or policy, and accounting such as consumed CPU time. These fields let the kernel find a task, decide its eligibility, and attribute resource use. Real systems often schedule threads and distribute process-level state among shared objects, so there is not necessarily one monolithic structure containing every field described by a textbook diagram.

the-process-control-block.title: Saved context is different from the address space
the-process-control-block.body: Registers and the instruction position describe where an execution resumes. Page-table and mapping references describe how its addresses are interpreted. Neither is a complete copy of application memory stored inside the task record. Switching between threads sharing one address space may preserve mapping context while restoring different register and stack state. Switching between processes can require changing both, subject to architecture-specific optimizations.

the-process-control-block.title: References connect the task to kernel objects
the-process-control-block.body: The task's record links to descriptors, credentials, signal state, memory mappings, and other managed objects. Multiple tasks can reference the same object with explicit sharing semantics. The object remains alive until its required ownership and operation references are released. This graph explains why ending a task, closing one descriptor, and destroying the final underlying object are different events rather than one universal cleanup operation.

the-process-control-block.title: Follow a blocking read through the task record
the-process-control-block.body: The task enters the kernel, discovers no data is available, records a wait condition, and becomes blocked. Its saved execution continuation and resource references remain valid. An arrival makes it runnable and places it under scheduling consideration. Later dispatch restores execution, the read obtains data, and the task returns to user space. Recording a runnable state is necessary for progress but is not itself CPU execution.

process-states.title: State 1: New — creation and admission
process-states.body: In the textbook five-state model, New means the system is creating an execution and establishing the resources needed to admit it. Identity, execution context, and resource references must be prepared before the scheduler treats it as ready. Admission moves New to Ready. Real kernels may expose finer internal stages or omit a separately visible New label; the conceptual model describes responsibility, not a mandatory set of tool output strings.

process-states.title: State 2: Ready — eligible but waiting for a CPU
process-states.body: Ready means all conditions for execution are satisfied except receiving CPU service. A ready task can be delayed by other runnable tasks, priority, affinity, quotas, or scheduling policy. Dispatch moves Ready to Running. A task does not become blocked simply because another task currently owns the CPU. Measuring runnable queue delay distinguishes a CPU-service problem from time spent waiting for external events.

process-states.title: State 3: Running — executing instructions now
process-states.body: Running means a processor is currently executing the task, whether in its user code or in kernel work on its behalf. Preemption or yielding can move it to Ready. Waiting for unavailable I/O or another required event can move it to Blocked. Completion can move it to Terminated. On a multiprocessor, several tasks may be Running simultaneously; each logical processor executes only its currently scheduled context at an instant.

process-states.title: State 4: Blocked — progress requires an event
process-states.body: Blocked, also called Waiting in many textbooks, means the task cannot proceed until a condition such as data availability, a timer, or synchronization event is satisfied. Event completion normally moves Blocked to Ready, followed later by dispatch to Running. The event does not reserve a CPU automatically. A wakeup can also be spurious or lose a race for the resource, so the resumed operation may need to test its condition again.

process-states.title: State 5: Terminated — execution has ended
process-states.body: Terminated means the task will not resume ordinary execution. The system releases execution resources and records the required completion information. In Unix process management, a zombie can retain waitable termination information until reaped; it is not a sixth actively executing phase. Some diagrams add suspended states for swapped or administratively suspended tasks. Those extensions should be named explicitly instead of silently replacing the five-state model.

process-states.title: Complete transition example and operating-system labels
process-states.body: A worker follows New → Ready → Running → Blocked while awaiting disk data, then Ready → Running after completion, then Terminated. A time slice can introduce Running → Ready → Running without any I/O. Linux process displays commonly use R for runnable/running and distinguish several sleep, stop, and zombie states, so tool labels do not map one-to-one to textbook names. Always distinguish a conceptual lifecycle from implementation-specific state encodings.

fork-exec-wait-exit.title: fork: two return paths and inherited resources
fork-exec-wait-exit.body: A successful fork returns the child's identifier in the parent and zero in the child. Private memory begins with equivalent contents, commonly implemented with copy-on-write, while inherited descriptors refer to the same underlying open file descriptions. The child contains only the calling thread when the parent was multithreaded. Library and lock state copied from other threads can therefore be unusable in the child before exec.

fork-exec-wait-exit.title: exec: replacement succeeds without returning
fork-exec-wait-exit.body: An exec-family operation replaces the current execution image when successful, so the old code after that call does not run. On failure it returns to the old image with an error. The child must report that failure and terminate appropriately instead of continuing the parent's control path. In a multithreaded fork child, respect the restricted set of safe operations before exec; arbitrary allocation or logging can encounter inherited locked state.

fork-exec-wait-exit.title: wait: collect and interpret the outcome
fork-exec-wait-exit.body: The parent uses a wait interface to collect status for eligible children. It distinguishes normal exit from termination by signal through the interface's status interpretation macros rather than treating the raw status integer as an exit code. A nonblocking wait can report that no child is ready yet. If several children exit close together, reap all available outcomes; one notification should not be assumed to correspond to exactly one child.

fork-exec-wait-exit.title: exit and _exit serve different cleanup paths
fork-exec-wait-exit.body: Returning from main normally leads through language or C runtime termination, which can flush buffered streams and run registered cleanup. The low-level _exit path ends execution without those user-space cleanup actions. A child that cannot exec often needs the latter to avoid flushing copies of the parent's buffered output. Neither interface automatically means buffered file data is durable on storage; persistence requires the relevant file-system operations and guarantees.

clone-and-what-fork-shares.title: Address-space sharing with CLONE_VM
clone-and-what-fork-shares.body: Linux task creation can request a shared address space rather than a private fork-style image. With CLONE_VM, writes to shared mappings and address-space changes are visible through the shared memory context. This enables thread-like execution, but stacks and thread-local state still need correct setup. Hand-assembling a task with selected flags is not equivalent to satisfying a language runtime's complete thread-creation contract.

clone-and-what-fork-shares.title: Descriptor and filesystem context flags
clone-and-what-fork-shares.body: CLONE_FILES shares the descriptor table itself, so opening or closing entries affects the shared table. CLONE_FS shares filesystem-related context such as the current directory and root. Without table sharing, inherited descriptors can still reference common open file descriptions, producing shared offsets. Predict the exact operation: closing an entry, advancing an offset, and changing a current directory affect different objects.

clone-and-what-fork-shares.title: Signal and thread-group relationships
clone-and-what-fork-shares.body: CLONE_SIGHAND and CLONE_THREAD participate in signal-handler and thread-group relationships, with flag dependencies enforced by the kernel. Sharing signal dispositions does not imply that each task has the same blocked-signal mask. Linux exposes both process-level and thread-level identities in relevant APIs. Use established threading libraries for ordinary applications, since they coordinate these kernel choices with TLS, synchronization, cancellation, and runtime bookkeeping.

clone-and-what-fork-shares.title: Worked sharing matrix
clone-and-what-fork-shares.body: Imagine A and B share memory but have separate descriptor tables referring to one open file description. A writes a shared variable, and B can observe it with proper synchronization. A closes its descriptor, but B's table entry remains. B's later file read can still advance the common offset. If the table were shared instead, A's close would remove that table entry for both tasks. Sharing must be evaluated per object.

zombies-and-orphans.title: Zombie lifetime ends through reaping
zombies-and-orphans.body: When a child exits, its parent may still need its status and accounting information. The retained waitable record is the zombie. It does not continue running the old application instructions or retain the full active address space merely because its PID remains visible. Reaping consumes the termination information through the wait mechanism. Sending another termination signal to a zombie cannot make an already finished execution finish again.

zombies-and-orphans.title: An orphan can still be actively running
zombies-and-orphans.body: Orphaning concerns the parent-child relationship, not whether the child has stopped. When a parent exits, eligible descendants are reparented according to the system's adoption rules, including Linux subreapers and PID namespaces. The new responsible process must handle waitable children. This differs from a job-control orphaned process group, which has a specific session-related definition and should not be confused with every child whose original parent died.

zombies-and-orphans.title: Signals can coalesce while exits accumulate
zombies-and-orphans.body: Ordinary SIGCHLD notifications do not provide an unlimited one-notification-per-child queue. If several children terminate before a handler or event loop acts, the supervisor should repeatedly perform the appropriate nonblocking wait until no more relevant outcomes are available. Keep the actual child table and exit statuses as authoritative state. Notification count alone cannot tell the supervisor which operations succeeded or how many children remain.

zombies-and-orphans.title: Supervisor shutdown needs a reaping plan
zombies-and-orphans.body: A supervisor first stops creating new children, asks existing children to terminate according to policy, waits for bounded completion, and reaps each outcome. A forced termination step can be necessary for unresponsive children, but it does not remove the obligation to collect their status. Record child identity carefully so a stale numeric PID is not confused with a newly reused identifier during a long-lived management operation.

context-switching.title: Voluntary and involuntary switches
context-switching.body: A task can stop running because it blocks or yields, often classified as a voluntary switch, or because the scheduler preempts it, commonly classified as involuntary. Exact accounting follows the operating system's definitions. A high voluntary-switch count can indicate a healthy I/O-driven server, while runnable delay and involuntary switches can accompany CPU competition. Interpret the reason and workload rather than assigning one universal meaning to the total count.

context-switching.title: What execution context must survive
context-switching.body: The scheduler and architecture code preserve the state required to resume execution: stack position, registers as required by the switching convention, and relevant CPU or thread state. An address-space change may update translation context, but tagged translations can reduce unnecessary invalidation. The entire process memory is not copied on each switch. Describing a switch as copying every allocated byte substantially overstates what the mechanism does.

context-switching.title: Warm state can cost more than register bookkeeping
context-switching.body: The incoming task may not find its instructions, data, or translations in fast structures. A migrated task can also access remote NUMA memory or lose cache locality. These indirect costs depend on working-set size, sharing, hardware, and scheduling history. A microbenchmark that alternates two tiny tasks measures a different situation from switching among large server workers with disjoint memory footprints.

context-switching.title: Estimate overhead with an explicit model
context-switching.body: If a simplified switch costs 5 microseconds and useful service lasts 1 millisecond between switches, the modeled switching fraction is 5 divided by 1005, about 0.5 percent. With only 20 microseconds of useful service it becomes 5 divided by 25, or 20 percent. Real costs vary and include indirect effects, but the arithmetic shows why excessive fine-grained scheduling can dominate useful work.

signals.title: Disposition, mask, and pending state
signals.body: A disposition specifies default action, ignoring, or a handler for a signal. The blocked-signal mask is per thread, while dispositions are generally shared within the process. A generated signal can remain pending until an eligible thread can handle it. A process-directed signal may be delivered to one eligible thread rather than every thread. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored under normal POSIX signal rules.

signals.title: Standard and real-time signals differ
signals.body: Repeated pending instances of an ordinary signal can coalesce, so a handler cannot reliably count arbitrary events from delivery count alone. POSIX real-time signals have queuing and ordering guarantees within their defined limits and can carry small associated values. Neither category is an unlimited durable job store. Use a queue or recorded state for work and use signals as the notification mechanism where that design is appropriate.

signals.title: Handlers must respect interrupted library state
signals.body: A handler can interrupt code while a library lock is held. Calling a non-async-signal-safe function that needs the same state can deadlock or corrupt it. A common approach records minimal signal-safe state or writes a notification through a suitable safe mechanism, then lets the normal event loop perform cleanup. In multithreaded programs, a dedicated synchronous signal-waiting thread can simplify ownership when masks are configured consistently.

signals.title: Interrupted operations and restart policy
signals.body: Some blocking operations return an interruption error after a handler runs, while others can restart under applicable flags and API rules. A loop must distinguish interruption before progress from a short successful result after partial progress. Blindly restarting the original write length can duplicate bytes already written. Shutdown handlers should also be designed so restarting a blocked operation does not accidentally prevent the program from observing its termination request.

process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.title: A process group represents a controllable job
process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.body: A shell can place related pipeline processes in one process group so it can signal or manage them together. The group identifier is separate from each member's PID, although a group leader's PID commonly establishes the group's identity. Sending an interrupt to only one stage of a pipeline can leave the others running. Job control therefore operates on the group that represents the user's logical command.

process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.title: A session organizes terminal relationships
process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.body: A session contains process groups and can have a controlling terminal. Its foreground process group receives terminal-generated job-control signals and has special access to terminal input under the relevant rules. A process group and a session are not synonyms: several jobs can belong to one shell session. Creating a new session changes these relationships and is one ingredient in daemonization, not a universal complete daemon setup.

process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.title: Foreground, background, stop, and continue
process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.body: A foreground job owns the shell's terminal interaction until it finishes or stops. A background job can continue execution while the shell accepts another command, but terminal reads and writes can be restricted by job-control settings. Stop suspends execution without terminating the job, and continue makes it eligible to resume. A stopped task still needs resources and bookkeeping even though it is not currently consuming ordinary CPU execution.

process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.title: Worked pipeline control
process-groups-sessions-and-jobs.body: For producer | filter | consumer, the shell can create three child processes in one process group and connect them with pipes. A terminal interrupt targets the foreground group, affecting the entire job according to each member's signal handling. After a stop, the shell regains foreground control and records the job. Resuming in foreground involves both continuing the group and restoring its terminal relationship, rather than merely running another copy of the command.

why-scheduling-exists.title: CPU bursts alternate with waiting
why-scheduling-exists.body: A task commonly computes for a burst, then waits for input, a timer, a lock, or a device. Scheduling lets another ready task use the CPU during that wait. CPU-bound and I/O-bound are workload tendencies, not permanent process types: a single program can alternate between both. The scheduler cannot accelerate a dependency by running a blocked task, because that task has no useful instruction path until its condition changes.

why-scheduling-exists.title: Preemption supports responsiveness
why-scheduling-exists.body: Without preemption, a task that never voluntarily blocks can retain a CPU indefinitely under a cooperative policy. Timer and scheduling mechanisms let the OS interrupt execution and provide service to others. Preemption requires saving resumable state and coordinating shared kernel structures. It improves control over response time but does not by itself guarantee fairness, deadlines, or absence of priority inversion; those depend on policy and synchronization.

why-scheduling-exists.title: Policy balances competing objectives
why-scheduling-exists.body: High throughput, low first-response time, short total completion time, fairness, predictable deadlines, energy use, and cache locality can conflict. Running one large batch task uninterrupted may maximize its locality while making interactive jobs wait. Frequently alternating all tasks may improve early response while increasing overhead. Choose metrics tied to the application's goal rather than claiming one scheduler is best without specifying workload and constraints.

why-scheduling-exists.title: Scheduling is not admission control
why-scheduling-exists.body: If work arrives faster than the available CPUs can execute it, a scheduler can redistribute waiting but cannot create missing capacity. With an average 2 ms of CPU per request, one fully available CPU has a simplified upper bound of 500 requests per second before overhead. Sustained arrivals above that require queuing, rejection, reduced work, or more effective CPU capacity. Priority changes decide who suffers, not whether overload exists.

scheduling-metrics.title: Define arrival, first service, and completion
scheduling-metrics.body: Let A be arrival time, S the first instant receiving CPU service, and C completion. Response time is S minus A, while turnaround time is C minus A. They measure different experiences: a task can respond promptly and still finish much later after preemption. State whether the workload includes I/O and whether arrival means external request arrival or entry into the scheduler's ready queue.

scheduling-metrics.title: Waiting time must match the workload model
scheduling-metrics.body: For a CPU-only job with total CPU burst B and no other waits, ready-queue waiting time is C minus A minus B. If the job also blocks for I/O, subtracting only B incorrectly counts device waiting as scheduler waiting. Track the intervals directly: running, runnable, and blocked. This distinction matters when deciding whether more CPUs or a faster dependency can improve observed response latency.

scheduling-metrics.title: Worked FCFS metrics
scheduling-metrics.body: Suppose A arrives at 0 with burst 5 and B arrives at 1 with burst 2. Under nonpreemptive FCFS with zero switch cost, A runs from 0 to 5 and B from 5 to 7. A's response and waiting are 0 and turnaround 5. B's response and waiting are 4 and turnaround 6. Mean waiting is 2, while mean turnaround is 5.5; these averages should not be confused.

scheduling-metrics.title: Throughput, utilization, and distributions
scheduling-metrics.body: Throughput counts completed jobs per time interval; CPU utilization measures the fraction of capacity doing accounted execution. Neither guarantees low tail latency. A system can remain fully utilized while a low-priority job starves. Report percentiles or worst cases when deadlines or interactive responsiveness matter, and specify whether measurements include warmup and unfinished jobs. Dropping unfinished jobs from averages can conceal the worst scheduling outcomes.

fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.title: FCFS: arrival order and the convoy effect
fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.body: First-come, first-served runs ready jobs in arrival order without preempting a current CPU burst in the basic model. With three jobs arriving together in order A=8, B=2, C=1, completion times are 8, 10, and 11, and waits are 0, 8, and 10. Short jobs wait behind the long burst. This convoy effect can harm responsiveness even when the scheduling rule is easy to implement.

fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.title: SJF: choose the shortest eligible burst
fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.body: Nonpreemptive shortest-job-first selects the smallest known next CPU burst among ready jobs. For the same simultaneous arrivals, order C=1, B=2, A=8 gives waits 0, 1, and 3, averaging 4/3 instead of 6 under the stated FCFS order. The favorable result assumes known bursts and no switching cost. Real systems must estimate future bursts, and repeatedly arriving short jobs can delay a long job.

fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.title: SRTF: reconsider when new work arrives
fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.body: Shortest-remaining-time-first is the preemptive version. Let A arrive at 0 with burst 8 and B arrive at 1 with burst 2. A runs for 1, then B's remaining 2 is shorter than A's remaining 7, so B runs from 1 to 3 and A finishes at 10. B's waiting is 0 and A's waiting is 2. Nonpreemptive SJF would not interrupt A merely because B arrived.

fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.title: Prediction and starvation change the engineering decision
fcfs-sjf-and-srtf.body: A scheduler can estimate a next burst using a weighted combination of recent observed bursts and earlier history, but a prediction is not a guarantee. Interactive behavior and phase changes can make past measurements misleading. Aging or service guarantees can bound neglect of long jobs. Compare the benefit of early short-job completion against preemption costs, estimation error, and fairness requirements before adopting the idealized model as a production policy.

round-robin.title: The ready queue rotates after a quantum
round-robin.body: Round robin dispatches a ready task for at most a time quantum. If it finishes or blocks sooner, another task can run immediately. If it consumes the quantum and remains runnable, it normally joins the end of the ready queue under the simple model. A blocked task is not assigned empty turns while it waits. The quantum is an upper service slice, not a requirement to waste unused CPU time.

round-robin.title: Complete worked schedule
round-robin.body: Take A=5, B=3, and C=1 CPU units, all arriving at 0, quantum 2, and zero switch overhead. The execution intervals are A 0–2, B 2–4, C 4–5, A 5–7, B 7–8, and A 8–9. Completion times are A=9, B=8, C=5. Waiting times are completion minus burst: 4, 5, and 4. First-response times are 0, 2, and 4.

round-robin.title: Quantum size changes response and overhead
round-robin.body: A very large quantum approaches FCFS behavior for short bursts. A very small quantum causes frequent switches, improving early service distribution but potentially spending too much time on switching and disrupting caches. If ten ready tasks each receive 2 ms, one task may wait roughly nine other quanta before its next turn in the simple steady model. Arrivals, blocking, priorities, and switch cost change that estimate.

round-robin.title: Fair slices do not imply equal application progress
round-robin.body: Two tasks receiving equal CPU duration may complete different amounts of useful work because their instructions, cache misses, and dependencies differ. Threads belonging to one application can also receive more aggregate service if fairness is defined per task rather than per group. State the fairness unit and resource boundary. Round-robin service is a CPU scheduling property, not a promise of equal request throughput or identical completion times.

priority-scheduling-and-aging.title: Define priority direction and preemption explicitly
priority-scheduling-and-aging.body: A priority scheduler selects the highest-priority eligible task, but numeric conventions vary: a smaller number can mean higher priority in one interface and the opposite in another. A preemptive policy can interrupt a lower-priority running task when higher-priority work becomes ready. A nonpreemptive variant waits for the current burst to end or block. State both choices before drawing the schedule.

priority-scheduling-and-aging.title: Starvation under an endless high-priority stream
priority-scheduling-and-aging.body: If high-priority jobs keep arriving quickly enough to keep the CPU busy, a ready lower-priority task may never be selected. It can be runnable for a long time without being deadlocked or blocked on I/O. This is starvation caused by policy. Increasing the low-priority task's time quantum does not help if it never receives a turn; selection and service duration are different decisions.

priority-scheduling-and-aging.title: Aging changes eligibility over time
priority-scheduling-and-aging.body: Aging raises the effective priority of tasks that have waited, with a rule for when the increase resets or decays after service. In a toy scheme, a task improves one priority level after each 10 ms of ready waiting. A task initially four levels behind can eventually compete if the allowed range permits it. A useful policy also defines ties, bounds, and treatment of blocked time so aging cannot be gamed trivially.

priority-scheduling-and-aging.title: Priority inversion requires another mechanism
priority-scheduling-and-aging.body: A high-priority task waiting on a lock held by a low-priority task can be delayed by medium-priority work that prevents the owner from running. Raising priority based only on long waiting may be too slow for the dependency. Priority inheritance temporarily boosts the owner under appropriate mutex protocols. Aging addresses prolonged lack of CPU selection; inheritance addresses a specific ownership dependency. They solve related but distinct scheduling problems.

multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.title: Fixed multilevel queues separate classes
multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.body: A fixed multilevel queue policy assigns work to classes such as interactive and batch, each with its own internal scheduling rule. A separate rule allocates CPU between classes, perhaps strict priority or weighted shares. If membership never changes, an incorrectly classified task retains that treatment. Strict priority between queues can starve lower queues even when each individual queue uses a fair rule internally.

multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.title: Feedback queues adapt to observed behavior
multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.body: A multilevel feedback queue allows tasks to move between queues based on their service history. A common teaching design starts new tasks high, gives short quanta there, and demotes tasks that consume their allotted CPU budget. Lower levels may use longer quanta to reduce overhead for CPU-heavy work. This favors quick responses without requiring exact future burst lengths, but every demotion and promotion rule must be stated.

multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.title: Account for cumulative service and periodic boosts
multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.body: If a task avoids demotion merely by yielding just before a quantum expires, it can game a naive feedback scheduler. Charging cumulative service within a level prevents this loophole. Periodic priority boosts can let long-waiting tasks make progress and accommodate workload phase changes. Boost frequency and accounting windows trade responsiveness against fairness; there is no single universal MLFQ configuration shared by all systems.

multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.title: Worked feedback trace
multilevel-queues-and-mlfq.body: Use Q0 with a 2-unit budget and Q1 with a 4-unit budget. A new CPU-bound task runs 2 units in Q0, remains unfinished, and moves to Q1. An interactive task arriving in Q0 can then receive service before the lower-queue task under strict interqueue priority. If the interactive task blocks after 1 unit, its remaining-budget handling depends on the stated policy. Without that rule, the schedule is underspecified.

multiprocessor-scheduling.title: Shared and per-CPU run queues
multiprocessor-scheduling.body: A shared run queue makes eligible work visible in one place but can create synchronization and cache contention as CPU count grows. Per-CPU queues improve local access but require load balancing so one CPU does not remain idle while another has excess runnable work. Real policies can combine hierarchy and locality. Queue length alone is imperfect because tasks differ in service demand and eligibility.

multiprocessor-scheduling.title: Affinity preserves locality but can restrict capacity
multiprocessor-scheduling.body: A task's recent CPU may retain its cache and translation working set. Keeping affinity can reduce warmup cost, while hard pinning can prevent the task from using an otherwise idle CPU. If four workers are pinned to one CPU on a four-CPU machine, unused processors do not eliminate their ready-queue delay. Distinguish an advisory placement preference from an enforced CPU mask before diagnosing imbalance.

multiprocessor-scheduling.title: NUMA and simultaneous multithreading
multiprocessor-scheduling.body: NUMA systems attach memory to nodes with different access costs from different CPUs. Moving execution without moving or sharing its data can increase remote-memory traffic. Simultaneous multithreading exposes logical CPUs that share execution resources, so two logical CPUs are not always equivalent to two independent physical cores. Placement decisions should consider topology, working sets, and memory bandwidth rather than treating every processor identifier as identical capacity.

multiprocessor-scheduling.title: Load balancing has a cost
multiprocessor-scheduling.body: Suppose one CPU has a long queue and another is idle. Migrating a task can reduce waiting, but requires coordination and may sacrifice useful cached state. For tiny tasks, migration overhead can exceed saved delay; for sustained imbalance, refusing migration wastes capacity. Measure both runnable latency and application throughput across a representative interval. A perfectly equal queue length at every instant is not itself the objective.

real-time-scheduling.title: Deadlines define correctness requirements
real-time-scheduling.body: A hard real-time system treats a missed deadline as an unacceptable failure under its design assumptions. Soft real-time work degrades in usefulness or quality when late. Fast average response does not establish either guarantee. Specify each task's execution budget, release pattern, deadline, and blocking behavior, then consider worst-case interference rather than only an unloaded demonstration in which every operation happened to finish quickly.

real-time-scheduling.title: Rate-monotonic scheduling
real-time-scheduling.body: For independent periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods under the classic single-CPU model, rate-monotonic priority gives shorter periods higher priority. A sufficient utilization bound for n such tasks is n times (2^(1/n) minus 1), under the model's assumptions. Failing this sufficient bound does not prove infeasibility. Blocking, release jitter, overhead, and differing deadlines require a more appropriate schedulability analysis than this introductory formula.

real-time-scheduling.title: Earliest-deadline-first and an example
real-time-scheduling.body: EDF selects the ready job with the nearest absolute deadline. For ideal independent preemptible periodic work with deadlines equal to periods on one CPU, total utilization no greater than one is the familiar feasibility condition. Tasks with execution/period values 1/4 and 2/5 use 0.25 + 0.4 = 0.65 of the CPU. This arithmetic omits blocking and overhead; it cannot be used as an unconditional real-machine guarantee.

real-time-scheduling.title: Bounding work includes locks and I/O
real-time-scheduling.body: A task can miss a deadline while using little CPU if it waits on an unbounded lock, storage request, page fault, or lower-priority owner. Real-time engineering includes bounded critical sections, suitable synchronization protocols, memory behavior, admission control, and overload policy. Assigning a high priority to every thread is not sufficient and can starve essential background work. Measure worst-case paths under the constraints the design actually promises.

linux-scheduling-classes.title: Normal policies and fair service
linux-scheduling-classes.body: Linux normal tasks commonly use SCHED_OTHER, also called SCHED_NORMAL internally, with niceness influencing relative weight in fair scheduling. SCHED_BATCH and SCHED_IDLE provide other non-real-time policy choices. A nice value is not a millisecond deadline or an absolute reservation. Effective service also depends on competing runnable tasks, CPU affinity, control-group policy, and the kernel configuration in use.

linux-scheduling-classes.title: SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR
linux-scheduling-classes.body: SCHED_FIFO is a fixed-priority real-time policy without a normal time-slice rotation among same-priority tasks unless a task blocks, yields, or is otherwise displaced according to the policy. SCHED_RR adds round-robin time slicing among equal-priority real-time tasks. Higher-priority eligible work can preempt lower-priority work. Neither policy means the application is guaranteed to meet deadlines without resource and blocking analysis.

linux-scheduling-classes.title: SCHED_DEADLINE expresses a reservation contract
linux-scheduling-classes.body: SCHED_DEADLINE uses runtime, deadline, and period parameters within Linux's deadline-scheduling and bandwidth-control mechanisms. Runtime bounds the service budget associated with the reservation. Admission checks and permissions constrain use; selecting the policy is not simply assigning a priority number. The task must still execute within its budget and avoid uncontrolled dependencies. Verify details against the deployed kernel and permitted scheduling domain before choosing parameters.

linux-scheduling-classes.title: Policy choice, permissions, and observation
linux-scheduling-classes.body: Inspect a task's actual policy, priority, affinity, and resource controls rather than inferring behavior from its source code or process name. Real-time configuration typically requires appropriate privileges or limits, and a failed policy-setting call must be handled. A process can request one policy but continue under another if the application ignores an error. Record the effective configuration alongside measurements when comparing scheduling behavior.

fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.title: CFS and weighted virtual runtime
fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.body: The classic CFS explanation tracks service through virtual runtime, advancing it according to how much CPU a task received relative to its weight. A task with less virtual service is favored to approximate proportional sharing over time. Niceness affects weight rather than granting a fixed wall-clock slice in every cycle. This is a conceptual model of fair service, not a promise that every runnable task receives exactly identical short-term latency.

fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.title: EEVDF separates eligibility from selection
fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.body: EEVDF uses lag to reason about whether a task is owed service relative to an ideal share. Eligible tasks have nonnegative lag in the basic explanation. Among them, the scheduler selects the earliest virtual deadline, allowing requested service size to influence responsiveness. A task's virtual deadline is a fair-scheduling construct; it is not an application hard deadline like a sensor response that must occur before a particular wall-clock time.

fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.title: Worked eligibility example
fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.body: Suppose A has positive lag and virtual deadline 30, B has negative lag and deadline 10, and C has zero lag and deadline 20 in a simplified snapshot. B's earlier deadline does not make it eligible because it has already exceeded its share. Among eligible A and C, C's deadline is earlier. This example illustrates the two decisions; real arithmetic, time advancement, and queue handling follow the kernel implementation.

fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.title: Version-sensitive behavior and sleeping tasks
fair-scheduling-cfs-to-eevdf.body: Linux has been transitioning its fair scheduler from the earlier CFS selection approach to EEVDF, and details continue to evolve. Brief sleeps must not let a task repeatedly erase excess service and gain an unfair advantage, so lag handling across sleep matters. Check the deployed kernel documentation and source for exact accounting and available controls. Do not present one release's internal data structure or tuning interface as a permanent cross-version contract.

what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.title: Per-thread execution state
what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.body: Each kernel-scheduled thread needs its own instruction position, register context, stack, scheduling state, and identity for relevant kernel operations. This is enough for one thread to stop while another continues. The process supplies shared relationships such as the address space and many resources. A thread is therefore an independent execution path within a resource-sharing arrangement, not merely a function that happens to run quickly.

what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.title: Thread-local storage and shared memory
what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.body: Thread-local storage gives each thread a distinct instance of selected variables, but ordinary heap and global objects remain shared within the process. A stack is conventionally owned by one thread, yet another thread can access it if given a pointer and if lifetime and synchronization rules permit. Private-by-convention is different from protected-by-page-table isolation. Thread-local data also requires correct initialization and teardown by the runtime.

what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.title: Blocking and scheduling happen per execution
what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.body: If thread A waits for a lock or blocking I/O, it can become unschedulable while B remains runnable. The kernel can dispatch B even though both belong to one process. If the application uses only one carrier for many logical tasks, however, a blocking native call can strand unrelated logical tasks behind that carrier. Always identify whether the object called a thread is visible to the kernel or only to a runtime.

what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.title: Signals, exit, and the shared failure boundary
what-a-thread-is-to-the-kernel.body: Some events target an individual thread while others target the process or terminate the whole thread group according to platform rules. An invalid write by one thread can corrupt a shared object later used by another, even if the writer itself does not immediately crash. Normal thread return differs from terminating the entire process. Libraries must document which termination mechanism they use instead of treating all forms of exit as equivalent.

processes-vs-threads.title: Compare which state is shared
processes-vs-threads.body: Threads in one process generally share mappings, heap, globals, and open-resource tables, while each has its own execution stack and registers. Separate processes normally have distinct private mappings but can share file objects and explicit shared memory. Neither phrase, process or thread, answers every ownership question. Draw the objects and references for the actual design before assuming that all data is isolated or all handles are shared.

processes-vs-threads.title: Communication cost includes the data model
processes-vs-threads.body: Threads can pass a pointer to an existing object, but must coordinate mutation and lifetime. Process communication often serializes messages through pipes or sockets, providing a clearer ownership boundary at a copying cost. Shared-memory IPC avoids some copies while reintroducing synchronization and crash-consistency questions. Compare total work, including serialization, coordination, cache movement, and recovery, rather than counting only the number of boundary crossings.

processes-vs-threads.title: Security and recovery determine useful boundaries
processes-vs-threads.body: A separate process can be granted fewer credentials, filtered system calls, and bounded resources, making it a useful isolation unit. A thread usually cannot be trusted as a sandbox against other threads sharing its address space. Process isolation still requires safe IPC validation and appropriate privileges. If every worker inherits unrestricted authority and sensitive descriptors, simply creating more processes does not produce a well-designed security boundary.

processes-vs-threads.title: Worked server design comparison
processes-vs-threads.body: For a CPU-heavy parser processing untrusted input, process workers can be restarted after crashes without necessarily losing the supervisor. For a trusted in-memory pipeline sharing large mutable structures, threads can avoid repeated serialization if synchronization is correct. Either design needs bounded admission and response deadlines. The right choice depends on failure containment and data ownership; a benchmark of empty thread creation does not settle the application architecture.

user-and-kernel-threads.title: Many-to-one mapping
user-and-kernel-threads.body: Many user-level threads can share one kernel thread. Switching among them may avoid a kernel scheduling transition, but only one can execute at a time on that carrier. A blocking operation that the runtime cannot intercept can block them all. Multiple logical stacks do not create additional physical parallelism. Cooperative systems also require runnable tasks to yield or suspend so other tasks receive a chance to execute.

user-and-kernel-threads.title: One-to-one mapping
user-and-kernel-threads.body: Each application thread can correspond to a kernel-scheduled thread. A blocking thread then need not stop its peers, and different threads can run on separate CPUs. The cost includes kernel task state, stack resources, and scheduling competition when thread count grows. One-to-one mapping is not a reason to create an unbounded thread per request; waiting clients can still exhaust memory and descriptors before CPU capacity is saturated.

user-and-kernel-threads.title: Many-to-many mapping
user-and-kernel-threads.body: A runtime can multiplex many logical tasks across several kernel carriers. This combines lightweight logical waiting with physical parallelism up to available carrier and CPU capacity. The runtime needs scheduling queues, wakeup coordination, and rules for operations that pin or block carriers. Work stealing can balance logical tasks, but does not eliminate data dependencies, global locks, or NUMA costs. Kernel and runtime schedulers both influence observed latency.

user-and-kernel-threads.title: A blocked carrier changes the available parallelism
user-and-kernel-threads.body: Suppose 100 logical tasks run on four carriers. If three carriers enter long blocking native calls that the runtime does not compensate for, the remaining tasks share one carrier. The process may show low CPU use even with a large logical queue. Investigate carrier occupation and runtime state together. Increasing logical task count cannot restore the missing carriers and may only increase retained request memory.

thread-creation-and-teardown.title: Creation establishes a happens-before boundary
thread-creation-and-teardown.body: Thread creation communicates a start routine and argument under the threading API's synchronization guarantees. The caller must finish preparing shared input before publishing it and must keep referenced objects alive while the worker uses them. The new worker may run before the creator reaches its next source statement. Code must not depend on an assumed delay between requesting creation and the child's first instruction.

thread-creation-and-teardown.title: Joinable versus detached lifetime
thread-creation-and-teardown.body: A joinable thread retains completion information and relevant resources until another thread joins it according to the API contract. Joining can also synchronize the worker's completed writes with the joining thread. A detached thread releases its thread-lifecycle resources automatically after completion, but detachment does not keep the application's shared objects alive. It still needs an ownership protocol for every referenced queue, buffer, and synchronization object.

thread-creation-and-teardown.title: Cooperative cancellation protects invariants
