thread-creation-and-teardown.body: A worker can check a cancellation request between operations and leave through cleanup paths that release locks and references. Asynchronous termination at an arbitrary instruction can interrupt a multi-step invariant update. API cancellation points and cleanup handlers have specific contracts and are not interchangeable with killing a process. Decide what happens to accepted but unfinished work and how callers learn whether an operation completed before cancellation.

thread-creation-and-teardown.title: Order shutdown around shared objects
thread-creation-and-teardown.body: For a worker pool, stop admission, record shutdown under the queue's synchronization protocol, wake sleeping workers, and join them before destroying the queue and its mutexes. Workers should either drain accepted work or cancel it under a stated policy. Destroying a condition variable while a worker may still wait on it is a lifetime error. A successful shutdown requires both task completion accounting and thread completion accounting.

what-a-context-switch-costs.title: Separate runtime switches from kernel switches
what-a-context-switch-costs.body: A coroutine can yield to another logical task on the same carrier without asking the kernel to choose a different thread. A kernel context switch changes the scheduled execution context and may alter address-space or CPU-local state. Both can disrupt useful execution, but their bookkeeping paths differ. Benchmark reports should identify which event they measured rather than labeling every change in logical task a context switch with one universal cost.

what-a-context-switch-costs.title: Wakeup latency includes queueing
what-a-context-switch-costs.body: The interval from making a thread runnable to its first resumed instruction contains scheduler queue delay as well as dispatch work. Under contention, that queueing can dwarf the mechanical save-and-restore path. A synchronization ping-pong benchmark therefore measures wakeup, coordination, and scheduling interactions. Increasing a measured handoff time does not by itself prove that register saving became slower; it may reflect another runnable task receiving service first.

what-a-context-switch-costs.title: Placement changes the experiment
what-a-context-switch-costs.body: When two threads alternate on one CPU, the experiment emphasizes descheduling and redispatch on that CPU. On different CPUs, the threads can overlap and the shared synchronization data may bounce through the coherence system instead. NUMA placement, power states, frequency scaling, and virtualization further affect results. Keep these conditions fixed when comparing a code change, and report a distribution rather than only the minimum observed sample.

what-a-context-switch-costs.title: Use the measurement to choose work granularity
what-a-context-switch-costs.body: If dispatch and synchronization overhead consume a significant fraction of a tiny task, batching several items per handoff can improve throughput. Larger batches also delay later arrivals and can reduce fairness. Measure end-to-end request latency as well as total completions after batching. An optimization that halves switch count but doubles the oldest request's wait may be inappropriate for an interactive workload even when aggregate CPU efficiency improves.

thread-pools-and-sizing.title: CPU-bound work follows effective CPU capacity
thread-pools-and-sizing.body: For independent CPU-bound tasks, a worker count near the effective available CPU capacity is a useful starting point. Effective capacity can be lower than the machine's processor count because of affinity, container quotas, competing work, or shared hardware resources. Additional runnable workers can improve neither arithmetic throughput nor a saturated memory bus automatically. Measure the limiting resource before treating a larger pool as added computing power.

thread-pools-and-sizing.title: Use Little's law for outstanding work
thread-pools-and-sizing.body: In a stable system, average in-flight work is approximately throughput multiplied by average time in the system. At 200 requests per second and 0.05 seconds average residence, about 10 requests are present on average. This includes both waiting and execution as defined by the measured boundary. It is not automatically the required thread count, because asynchronous waits and batched processing can map requests to threads differently.

thread-pools-and-sizing.title: Bound queues by useful waiting time
thread-pools-and-sizing.body: A queue holding 10,000 requests is not useful when every request expires after one second and the service can finish only 500 per second. Admission should account for remaining deadlines and resource cost, not only item count. Rejection, caller backpressure, or a bounded wait can prevent wasted processing of already expired work. Separate pools can keep a stalled dependency from consuming every execution slot needed by unrelated operations.

thread-pools-and-sizing.title: Avoid pool-induced dependency deadlocks
thread-pools-and-sizing.body: Suppose every worker runs a parent task that submits a child to the same pool and then synchronously waits. If all workers are occupied by parents, no child can run, even though the queue contains work. More threads merely shifts the threshold. Use nonblocking composition, execute dependent work under a safe policy, or reserve appropriately separated capacity. The dependency graph matters as much as the pool's nominal maximum size.

runtime-threading-models.title: Tasks and futures describe work, not placement
runtime-threading-models.body: A task or future represents an operation and its eventual outcome; it does not necessarily own a kernel thread. A scheduler may execute parts of that task on one or several carriers across suspensions. Thread-local assumptions can therefore fail when logical work migrates. Use the runtime's documented context-propagation facilities for request identity and tracing instead of assuming one logical request always retains one native thread identity.

runtime-threading-models.title: Event loops and cooperative progress
runtime-threading-models.body: An event loop runs ready callbacks and arranges wakeups for operations that cannot complete yet. A callback performing long computation prevents the loop from processing other ready events until it yields or finishes. Declaring a function async does not make all its instructions preemptible. Break up cooperative work where appropriate or move CPU-heavy work to bounded parallel capacity, preserving cancellation and result ownership across that boundary.

runtime-threading-models.title: Native blocking and runtime compensation
runtime-threading-models.body: Some runtimes park logical tasks when supported operations block, freeing the carrier for other work. Native libraries, foreign calls, locks, or runtime-specific constraints can instead retain a carrier. Whether compensation creates more carriers depends on the runtime and version. Investigate the exact operation and implementation rather than assuming every file, socket, or synchronization call participates in the same lightweight-suspension mechanism.

runtime-threading-models.title: Safepoints, garbage collection, and observability
runtime-threading-models.body: Managed runtimes can coordinate threads for garbage collection, stack inspection, or code management. These pauses or coordination delays are additional to kernel scheduling. A kernel trace can show a thread not progressing without explaining the runtime reason. Combine runtime task dumps, allocation or pause metrics, and OS observations with aligned timestamps. Otherwise a runtime-wide pause may be misdiagnosed as a network timeout or insufficient kernel scheduling priority.

race-conditions-and-atomicity.title: A data race and a logical race are different
race-conditions-and-atomicity.body: A language-level data race involves unsynchronized conflicting accesses under that language's memory model and can make a C or C++ program undefined. A logical race can occur even when every access is individually synchronized, if the overall sequence violates the intended rule. Checking that a queue is nonempty under a lock, unlocking, then removing under another lock acquisition can race with another consumer between those two steps.

race-conditions-and-atomicity.title: Atomic read-modify-write preserves one update
race-conditions-and-atomicity.body: An atomic fetch-add combines reading, computing, and writing the same atomic object into one indivisible operation with a specified ordering mode. Two increments starting from 10 then produce distinct prior values and a final value 12, assuming no other operations. A separately atomic load followed by an atomic store still does not make the combined increment indivisible. Atomic access and atomic compound transformation must not be confused.

race-conditions-and-atomicity.title: Compare-and-swap and retry invariants
race-conditions-and-atomicity.body: Compare-and-swap changes a value only if it still matches an expected value, reporting whether the change succeeded. A loop recomputes a candidate after failure because another participant may have changed the state. Algorithms must also consider object lifetime and ABA: a value can change away and back while the underlying situation differs. Atomic pointer replacement alone does not prove that the referenced object remains safe to dereference.

race-conditions-and-atomicity.title: Protect the invariant's full boundary
race-conditions-and-atomicity.body: For a bounded queue, the item storage, head and tail positions, and count must remain mutually consistent. Protecting each field independently can expose combinations that never represent a valid queue. A lock around the whole operation is often the clearest correct starting point. Only replace it with finer-grained or lock-free coordination after specifying linearization points, memory ordering, reclamation, and the progress guarantee required by the application.

memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.title: Compiler and processor ordering both matter
memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.body: Source-code order is not a sufficient cross-thread communication protocol. Compilers and processors can reorder or overlap work while preserving the guarantees applicable to a valid single-threaded execution and the language memory model. Synchronization constrains what another thread may observe. Reason in terms of the language's happens-before relationships before translating them into architecture-specific fences; a pattern that appears to work on one CPU may remain invalid source code.

memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.title: Release/acquire publication with a concrete dependency
memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.body: A producer writes payload fields, then stores true to an atomic ready flag with release ordering. A consumer that observes that release through a suitable acquire load can then read the published payload under the required lifetime assumptions. A relaxed load/store flag does not establish the same publication relationship. Resetting and reusing the buffer requires another ownership protocol so the producer does not overwrite data while the consumer still reads it.

memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.title: Sequential consistency and relaxed counting
memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.body: Sequentially consistent atomic operations provide a stronger global ordering model for those operations, while relaxed atomics primarily provide atomicity and per-object coherence without publishing unrelated data. A statistics counter may need only relaxed increments if no payload is being published through it. Choosing a weaker order should follow a proof of the required relationship, not a general belief that all stronger ordering is unnecessary overhead.

memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.title: False sharing compared with true contention
memory-ordering-and-false-sharing.body: True sharing occurs when threads intentionally contend on the same logical data. False sharing occurs when independent hot variables occupy the same coherence unit, often a cache line, and writes cause ownership traffic anyway. Separating per-thread counters can help the latter, while sharding or redesigning the shared operation may be needed for the former. Aggregate counters periodically and measure the layout change; padding can increase footprint and harm other cache behavior.

mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.title: Mutex: ownership protects an invariant
mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.body: A mutex admits one owner to a critical section, and the owner must release it according to the mutex contract. All accesses that require the same invariant must follow the same locking rule. Acquiring a mutex only around writes does not protect an unsynchronized reader from observing partial updates. Keep the lock's scope aligned with the data relationship, and define a consistent order when an operation needs multiple mutexes.

mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.title: Semaphore: permits represent available capacity
mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.body: A counting semaphore starts with a number of permits. Acquiring consumes a permit or waits; releasing returns one according to the protocol. A semaphore initialized to three can limit access to three concurrent resource users. It does not inherently identify one exclusive owner or protect every shared data structure used by those users. Incorrect extra releases can inflate capacity, so successful acquisition and release paths need balanced accounting.

mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.title: Condition variable: wait for a protected predicate
mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.body: The condition is ordinary shared state, such as queue_not_empty, protected by a mutex. A waiter holds that mutex, checks the predicate in a loop, and uses the condition wait operation to release the mutex and wait atomically with the notification protocol. After wakeup it reacquires the mutex and checks again. Notifications are not stored work items; the predicate is the durable fact that prevents missed-work reasoning errors.

mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.title: Bounded producer-consumer queue with two conditions
mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.body: A producer locks the queue and waits while count equals capacity, then inserts, increments count, and signals not_empty. A consumer waits while count is zero, removes an item, decrements count, and signals not_full. Both release the mutex after updating the invariant. Shutdown adds another predicate that wakes all affected waiters so an empty queue can stop cleanly rather than leaving consumers waiting for items that will never arrive.

mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.title: Signal, broadcast, and spurious wakeups
mutexes-semaphores-and-condition-variabl.body: Signaling wakes an eligible waiter under the API's rules; broadcasting wakes all current waiters, which then compete to reacquire the mutex. A wakeup does not reserve the predicate for a specific thread, and spurious wakeups may occur. Use broadcast when a state transition can allow several different wait conditions to proceed, such as shutdown. Excessive broadcasting can create contention, but replacing the predicate loop with an if statement is not a valid optimization.

how-blocking-works.title: The wait condition must remain authoritative
how-blocking-works.body: A waiting thread first determines whether progress is possible from protected shared state. It registers its interest and sleeps only through a protocol that closes the race with a producer changing that state. The wakeup is a prompt to inspect the condition again, not proof that the resource is still available. Another awakened participant may consume the resource before this thread obtains CPU service or the protecting lock.

how-blocking-works.title: Atomic compare-and-wait closes a dangerous gap
how-blocking-works.body: For Linux futex waiting, a waiter supplies the value it expects at a shared futex word. The kernel checks that value as part of the wait operation and does not sleep on a stale expectation if it has already changed. This helps avoid a producer updating state and waking just before the consumer parks. The futex is a building block; the surrounding atomics, state encoding, and lifetime still must form a correct synchronization protocol.

how-blocking-works.title: Wakeup, ownership, and scheduling are separate
how-blocking-works.body: An unlock operation changes ownership state and may wake one or more waiters. A woken thread becomes runnable but still needs CPU service and may need to compete again for acquisition. Some synchronization designs explicitly hand off ownership, while others permit barging by a new contender. Fairness and performance depend on that policy. A generic kernel wake operation should not be described as automatically transferring the protected resource.

how-blocking-works.title: Timeouts and cancellation race with success
how-blocking-works.body: A waiter can reach its deadline at nearly the same time that the condition becomes true. The API and surrounding protocol must determine whether it acquired the resource, timed out, or needs to recheck state while holding the lock. Cleanup must remove or invalidate wait registration without losing a permit or leaving a stale pointer. A timeout return does not justify releasing a lock or permit that was never acquired.

spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.title: Use spinning only when the owner can progress
spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.body: A spin waiter consumes CPU checking acquisition state. If the holder is briefly executing on another CPU, this can avoid sleep-and-wakeup overhead. If the holder is descheduled or waiting for storage, spinning can waste substantial capacity. The relevant question is not simply whether the critical section has few source lines, but whether its execution and ownership duration are actually bounded under contention and preemption.

spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.title: Local interrupt exclusion and cross-CPU exclusion
spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.body: Disabling ordinary local interrupts prevents specified interrupt handlers on the current CPU from interrupting the protected region. It does not stop another CPU from accessing the same data. A lock can coordinate CPUs, while the appropriate interrupt-control variant prevents same-CPU interruption from trying to acquire a lock already held by the interrupted context. Both dimensions matter when a data structure is used in task and interrupt contexts.

spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.title: Sleeping while holding a spinning lock
spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.body: A context holding a raw spinning lock must not perform an operation that can sleep and schedule away under the relevant kernel rules. Otherwise other CPUs can spin while the owner is unable to release, and context assumptions may be violated. Move potentially blocking preparation outside the critical section or use a sleeping lock where the context permits it. Acquisition, callbacks, allocation flags, and error handling all need the same scrutiny.

spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.title: Linux PREEMPT_RT changes lock implementation details
spinlocks-and-interrupt-context.body: The source-level name spinlock_t does not imply identical behavior under every Linux configuration. PREEMPT_RT changes several lock implementations toward sleeping, priority-inheritance-aware mechanisms, while raw_spinlock_t retains raw spinning semantics. Follow the kernel's documented lock-type and nesting rules for the actual configuration. Teaching a generic spinning algorithm is useful, but it must not be mistaken for an unconditional claim about every API whose name includes spinlock.

deadlock.title: Coffman condition 1: mutual exclusion
deadlock.body: At least one relevant resource permits only one owner at a time. A mutex-protected object, exclusive device, or nonshareable capacity unit can create this condition. Making a truly shareable immutable resource need no exclusive owner removes that source of dependency, but some updates fundamentally need coordination. Mutual exclusion alone is not deadlock: a single short critical section with no cyclic dependency can complete normally.

deadlock.title: Coffman condition 2: hold and wait
deadlock.body: A participant already owns at least one resource while requesting another. Acquiring every required resource together before starting can prevent this condition, but may reduce utilization and require knowing the full request in advance. Releasing held resources before waiting is another approach only when partial work can be safely rolled back. Dropping a lock after mutating half an invariant is not valid deadlock prevention.

deadlock.title: Coffman condition 3: no preemption
deadlock.body: Resources cannot simply be taken away safely from their current owners; owners must release them according to the protocol. Memory capacity or transactions sometimes support rollback or revocation, but an arbitrary mutex-protected update cannot safely lose ownership halfway through. Cancellation must restore a valid state before releasing resources. A timeout changes how long a caller waits, not whether the system can reclaim ownership without corrupting work.

deadlock.title: Coffman condition 4: circular wait
deadlock.body: A cycle exists in which each participant waits for a resource held by the next participant. For two locks, A owns X and requests Y while B owns Y and requests X. A global acquisition order breaks circular wait when every participating path follows it. The order must include callbacks, teardown, and exceptional paths, because one reversed acquisition is enough to reintroduce the cycle.

deadlock.title: Detection with a wait-for graph
deadlock.body: For single-instance resources under the usual model, draw an edge from a waiting task to the task whose resource it needs. A cycle identifies a deadlock. With multiple interchangeable instances, a simple resource-allocation cycle alone is not sufficient; track available units, current allocations, and outstanding requests to see whether some participant can finish and release resources. Detection requires a consistent enough view to avoid mistaking transient waits for a permanent cycle.

deadlock.title: Avoidance and the safe-state test
deadlock.body: Avoidance grants requests only when the resulting state remains safe under declared maximum needs. In a one-resource example with 10 units, A holds 4 and may need 3 more, B holds 3 and may need 2 more, and 3 are free. B can receive 2, finish, and release 5; A can then finish. That completion order proves safety under these bounds. Safety is stronger than merely observing no deadlock right now.

deadlock.title: Unsafe does not mean already deadlocked
deadlock.body: With those same allocations, granting all 3 free units to a new C that still needs 1 more leaves A needing 3, B needing 2, and C needing 1 with zero available. If the declared needs materialize and no owner releases early, none can finish. The state lacks a safe completion sequence in the model, but participants need not already be waiting. Avoidance rejects risk based on future claims, while detection examines an existing wait situation.

deadlock.title: Recovery needs a correctness policy
deadlock.body: After detecting deadlock, a system may abort an operation, roll back a transaction, restart a participant, or choose another documented recovery strategy. Select a victim using cost and fairness considerations, and account for external side effects that cannot be undone automatically. Restarting a payment worker after uncertain completion, for example, requires operation identity to avoid duplicate effects. A watchdog that only kills tasks can restore activity while leaving application state inconsistent.

starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.title: Starvation: others finish while one waits indefinitely
starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.body: An unfair lock or strict priority policy can repeatedly favor new or urgent work and neglect an older waiter. The system still completes operations, which distinguishes starvation from a full deadlock. Remedies include queued fairness, aging, quotas, or bounded-service rules, depending on the resource. Measure per-request waiting and maximum delay; aggregate throughput can look excellent while a small class of work makes no progress.

starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.title: Livelock: active retries without useful completion
starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.body: Two participants can repeatedly detect a conflict, release resources, and retry at the same time, recreating the same conflict forever. They remain active and may consume CPU or network bandwidth, yet no operation finishes. Randomized backoff or asymmetric ownership can break the repeated pattern. Bound retries and expose failure when the underlying condition persists, since adding delay alone does not establish a guarantee of eventual success.

starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.title: Priority inversion through an ownership chain
starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.body: Low-priority L owns a lock, high-priority H waits for it, and medium-priority M prevents L from running. H is indirectly delayed by M even though H outranks it. Priority inheritance raises L's effective priority while it blocks H, with propagation rules for chains under the chosen protocol. The boost ends according to ownership dependencies. It cannot make an unbounded critical section or stalled external I/O suddenly bounded.

starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.title: Choose the remedy from a concrete trace
starvation-livelock-and-priority-inversi.body: If a thread never acquires a frequently released lock, inspect fairness. If both threads repeatedly release and retry, inspect symmetry and backoff. If an urgent waiter depends on a descheduled lower-priority owner, inspect inheritance or ceiling protocols. These symptoms can look similar in a timeout dashboard. Capture ownership, waiting relationships, and scheduling events before applying a generic increase in thread count or timeout duration.

pipes-and-fifos.title: Anonymous pipes connect inherited endpoints
pipes-and-fifos.body: A pipe creation operation supplies a read end and a write end referring to kernel buffering. A parent can create the pipe before starting children, redirect one child's output to the write end and another's input to the read end, and close its unused references. The pipe carries a byte stream, so a reader may obtain only part of one write or bytes from several writes in one read.

pipes-and-fifos.title: FIFO names persist independently of open connections
pipes-and-fifos.body: A FIFO gives unrelated processes a pathname through which they can connect to a pipe-like channel. The filesystem entry names the communication endpoint; it is not a regular file accumulating the written bytes on disk. Opening can block until the required peer appears unless nonblocking behavior changes the contract. Permissions and pathname ownership determine who can connect, while EOF depends on open writer references rather than merely the existence of the name.

pipes-and-fifos.title: Atomic writes do not create message-oriented reads
pipes-and-fifos.body: A pipe guarantees appropriate noninterleaving for writes up to PIPE_BUF under its specified rules. This prevents several writers' small records from intermixing, but does not promise that one read returns exactly one record. Use explicit framing, and distinguish PIPE_BUF atomicity from total pipe capacity. A larger write can be partial or interleaved under relevant conditions, so a multiwriter protocol cannot rely on arbitrary-sized writes remaining indivisible.

pipes-and-fifos.title: EOF, broken pipes, and backpressure
pipes-and-fifos.body: A reader sees EOF after buffered bytes are consumed and every write reference is closed. A writer with no readers encounters the broken-pipe behavior, including SIGPIPE and an error according to signal handling. With readers present but a full buffer, blocking writers wait and nonblocking writers may receive a would-block result. These are three different conditions: peer disappearance, orderly stream end, and temporary lack of buffer capacity.

shared-memory.title: Create, size, map, and define the layout
shared-memory.body: A shared-memory object must be created or opened, given sufficient size under its API, and mapped with the required visibility and access permissions. Participants agree on a versioned layout containing lengths, offsets, and synchronization metadata. A pointer from one process is usually unsuitable because another process can map the region at a different virtual address. Validate offsets against mapping size before dereferencing shared data.

shared-memory.title: Publication requires inter-process synchronization
shared-memory.body: Writing payload bytes and then changing an ordinary ready flag is not a portable publication protocol. Use synchronization designed for process-shared memory or a correctly specified atomic protocol, including required memory ordering. A mutex intended only for threads inside one process may not be valid for this use without process-shared configuration. The shared pages provide storage visibility; they do not automatically provide atomic compound operations or notification.

shared-memory.title: Ring-buffer indices and wraparound
shared-memory.body: For a bounded ring, producer and consumer positions distinguish occupied slots from free ones. If both indices wrap to the same small value, the protocol needs an additional rule to distinguish full from empty, such as a reserved slot, count, or generation. Multiple producers additionally need reservation and publication coordination. A slot must not be reused while a reader still owns it, even if another index has advanced.

shared-memory.title: Crash recovery and schema compatibility
shared-memory.body: If a process dies while updating shared metadata, other participants need a way to detect and recover or reject the inconsistent state. Robust mutexes can report owner death where supported, but the application must repair its invariant before declaring the state usable. Persisting a shared-memory name is not a transaction protocol. Version the layout so a newly deployed process does not interpret old bytes using incompatible field sizes or semantics.

message-queues-and-signals.title: Message queues preserve records
message-queues-and-signals.body: A message queue sends discrete payloads according to its API rather than an unframed stream. Capacity, maximum message size, ordering, priority selection, and lifetime differ between implementations such as POSIX and System V queues. A receiver must allocate a suitable buffer and handle empty-queue or full-queue results. Check the actual interface rather than assuming that all operating-system message queues provide identical ordering or persistence behavior.

message-queues-and-signals.title: Capacity turns a queue into a flow-control boundary
message-queues-and-signals.body: A bounded queue can make producers block, reject submission, or report would-block when full. The application must choose what to do with the unaccepted work and whether a deadline still permits waiting. A queue slot being freed proves only that a message was removed, not that its business operation completed. Acknowledgments and operation identifiers are separate protocol elements when completion must be tracked reliably.

message-queues-and-signals.title: Signals provide a different notification contract
message-queues-and-signals.body: A standard signal can indicate that state needs inspection, but repeated pending instances may merge. Real-time signals can carry limited values and have queuing semantics within system limits. Neither is an appropriate substitute for arbitrary large serialized job data. Keep the work in a queue or other authoritative structure and arrange notifications so a missed or coalesced hint cannot permanently hide existing work from the consumer.

message-queues-and-signals.title: Worked duplicate-processing boundary
message-queues-and-signals.body: A worker removes job J, commits its external effect, then crashes before acknowledging completion. The dispatcher cannot infer from missing acknowledgment that J did nothing. Resubmitting J needs a stable identifier and idempotent or deduplicated processing. Conversely acknowledging before the effect risks losing work after a crash. Message transport and application completion have different failure boundaries even when both processes run on the same host.

unix-domain-sockets.title: Stream, datagram, and sequenced-packet choices
unix-domain-sockets.body: Unix-domain stream sockets provide ordered bytes and require application framing. Datagram and sequenced-packet variants expose message-oriented behavior according to platform support and their specific contracts. All are local-host communication mechanisms, but they can differ in connection establishment, record boundaries, buffering, and supported ancillary data. Choose a type because its guarantees match the protocol rather than assuming the Unix-domain address family alone determines message semantics.

unix-domain-sockets.title: Pathname naming and access control
unix-domain-sockets.body: A pathname socket is reached through a filesystem name, so directory ownership, permissions, name collisions, and removal policy matter. Linux also has an abstract namespace with different lifetime and access characteristics; it is not a portable replacement for every pathname design. An application should not blindly remove an arbitrary existing filesystem object before binding. Establish ownership of the endpoint location and check the expected object type and deployment lifecycle.

unix-domain-sockets.title: Descriptor passing sends a reference, not an integer
unix-domain-sockets.body: Ancillary-data mechanisms such as SCM_RIGHTS can transfer access to an open file description. The receiver obtains its own descriptor number, which need not equal the sender's integer. Both sides then have close and ownership responsibilities, and received descriptors should be handled with appropriate inheritance policy. Passing a descriptor can intentionally delegate an already-open resource, so validation must consider what authority that object grants rather than only the small payload message.

unix-domain-sockets.title: Peer identity and protocol validation
unix-domain-sockets.body: Some Unix-domain APIs expose peer credentials that help a server authorize local clients. Local location does not make every client trustworthy: messages can still contain invalid lengths, unsupported operations, or unwanted descriptor types. Bind authorization to the actual peer and intended operation, then validate ancillary data as carefully as normal bytes. A privileged local service with an unchecked socket protocol can undermine the process isolation the OS otherwise provides.

network-sockets-and-the-kernel.title: Listener state and accepted connections are separate
network-sockets-and-the-kernel.body: A TCP server creates a socket, binds an endpoint, begins listening, and accepts established connections. accept returns a new socket for one connection while the listener remains available. Each accepted connection has its own protocol and buffer state. Closing one accepted descriptor should not accidentally close the listener or unrelated clients. Bind errors, accept errors, and per-connection read errors belong to different lifecycle stages.

network-sockets-and-the-kernel.title: Handshake backlog and accept backlog
network-sockets-and-the-kernel.body: A TCP stack tracks connection establishment and connections ready for application acceptance, with implementation-specific controls and exceptional mechanisms. On Linux, the listen backlog relates to established connections waiting for accept, while incomplete-handshake handling has other controls. Increasing one limit does not guarantee capacity at every stage. Inspect which queue is pressured and whether the application accepts, reads, and finishes requests fast enough before changing a backlog setting.

network-sockets-and-the-kernel.title: Send and receive buffers provide bounded elasticity
network-sockets-and-the-kernel.body: A successful send normally means the local stack accepted some bytes, not that the peer application consumed them. Receive buffering can hold data until the application reads it, subject to flow control and memory limits. Slow readers and slow networks can retain buffers for long periods. Bound per-connection output and propagate backpressure into the producer rather than letting application queues grow without limit above already bounded kernel buffers.

network-sockets-and-the-kernel.title: Follow one request across all queueing stages
network-sockets-and-the-kernel.body: A client may wait during connection setup, before accept, before a worker reads, inside an application queue, and while a response drains. Each wait has different counters and remedies. If accept happens promptly but worker execution starts late, raising the listener backlog will not remove that queueing delay. Correlate connection timestamps, accepted descriptor counts, worker queue age, and response completion to locate the actual constrained stage.

zero-copy-transfers.title: Ordinary buffered forwarding copies through user space
zero-copy-transfers.body: A simple read-then-write loop can copy file data from kernel-managed pages into a user buffer and then copy it back into kernel networking buffers. This consumes CPU and memory bandwidth in addition to storage and network work. The exact path depends on caching, offloads, and implementation. Use this as a baseline data-flow model, then identify exactly which copy a specialized interface avoids rather than claiming that all data movement disappears.

zero-copy-transfers.title: sendfile transfers between supported descriptors
zero-copy-transfers.body: sendfile can move a file range toward another supported endpoint without an application read buffer on suitable paths. The caller still tracks the requested offset and remaining count, checks short progress and errors, and handles nonblocking completion requirements. Source data must remain valid under the interface's lifetime rules. Changing the file concurrently with a transfer can create correctness issues independent of whether the byte path saved CPU copies.

zero-copy-transfers.title: splice uses pipe-based kernel data paths
zero-copy-transfers.body: Linux splice moves data between supported descriptors with a pipe endpoint participating in the transfer. It can let a program connect kernel data paths without repeatedly copying payload through application buffers. Support and behavior depend on the endpoint types; unsupported combinations can fail or use different paths. The pipe has bounded capacity, so a forwarding loop must still handle backpressure, partial transfer, EOF, and closure in both directions.

zero-copy-transfers.title: mmap is access to pages, not a universal send operation
zero-copy-transfers.body: mmap exposes backing pages through an address range, avoiding an explicit read into a separate application buffer for that access. Initial touches can fault, and later writes or invalidation need synchronization. Sending from the mapping can still involve copies depending on the networking path. Compare CPU time, faults, memory bandwidth, and throughput under warm and cold conditions; choosing mmap solely because it is described as zero-copy can worsen a workload dominated by faults or random access.

linux-windows-and-macos.title: Kernel families and user-space interfaces
linux-windows-and-macos.body: Linux applications commonly use POSIX-oriented libraries over Linux-specific kernel interfaces. Windows exposes Win32 and native object facilities, and macOS combines Darwin's kernel foundations with its higher-level frameworks. These are different contracts around common needs such as protected execution, virtual memory, and I/O. A claim that all Unix-like systems implement an identical syscall ABI is incorrect even when source-level functions look familiar.

linux-windows-and-macos.title: Descriptors, handles, and asynchronous lifetime
linux-windows-and-macos.body: A Unix descriptor is a small process-local integer indexing a descriptor table. Windows handles use a different object and access model; sockets also have their own API conventions. Completion-oriented interfaces can require buffers and operation state to survive until completion is observed. Translating close into the nearest-looking function without checking cancellation and pending-operation rules can introduce use-after-free or lost-completion bugs.

linux-windows-and-macos.title: Paths and file replacement are portability traps
linux-windows-and-macos.body: Case behavior, pathname syntax, sharing modes, and open-file deletion semantics vary by platform and file system. An application that replaces an open log file on one system may need different coordination elsewhere. Do not infer behavior from the operating-system brand alone: mounted file systems and configuration can change it. Test the exact open, rename, and removal sequence the application relies on.

linux-windows-and-macos.title: Build a capability-based portability layer
linux-windows-and-macos.body: Describe required behavior first: wait for socket readiness, submit an asynchronous read, signal a shutdown request, or launch a child with redirected output. Then implement each capability with native contracts and explicit ownership rules. Keep platform-specific errors observable rather than collapsing everything into a generic failure. A portable abstraction should document any guarantee it cannot provide consistently across supported systems.
